## 7. Discussion, Limitations, and Future Directions

Our results show that cognition-informed sparse adaptation can improve code generation while reducing the number of parameters updated during training. We next discuss why this selective adaptation may be effective, its current computational limitations, and directions
for extending sparsity beyond model adaptation.

##### Why selective adaptation can improve accuracy.

CogAdapt’s gains suggest that adaptation quality depends on where updates occur, not only on how many parameters receive gradients.
Model responses identify blocks relevant to each task, while human-derived difficulty priors control the adaptation budget.
Restricting each example’s updates to these blocks may reduce interference with representations useful for other tasks, while preserving the pretrained expert weights.
Human-derived task and token weights further concentrate supervision on examples and code regions associated with greater processing demand.
Together, these mechanisms may help a smaller per-example adaptation budget produce more useful updates.
CogAdapt’s improvements over both all-block fine-tuning and fixed sparse baselines support the value of task-dependent selection.

##### From sparse adaptation toward sparse computation.

CogAdapt reduces the number of parameters that are eligible for gradients for each training example, but the full backbone still participates in the forward pass.
Consequently, the reduction in wall-clock time and energy is smaller than the reduction in adaptation parameters.
This distinction suggests an important next step: connecting cognitively informed adaptation with conditional model execution.
For example, future systems could extend sparsity beyond standard MoE
routing. While an MoE model already selects only a subset of experts within
each MoE block, the full sequence of transformer blocks still participates in
the forward pass. A future system could additionally use human-informed
signals to decide which blocks or adapters should participate for a given
task, or whether some block-level computation can be skipped entirely.
Combining expert routing with conditional block or adapter activation, early
exiting, or other forms of dynamic execution could therefore translate
CogAdapt’s adaptation sparsity into larger training and inference savings.

## 8. Conclusion

We present CogAdapt, a cognition-informed framework that uses human attention and EEG signals to guide task-dependent sparse adaptation of MoE code models.
Our analysis shows that human processing and model computation correspond both at individual code regions and across model depth, although the specific patterns differ between architectures.
Rather than assuming a single universally aligned layer, CogAdapt transfers these cognitive signals as priors to guide what training examples and code regions receive more emphasis and where adaptation occurs within the model.

Across two MoE backbones and two code-generation benchmarks, CogAdapt
achieves the best pass@1 among the evaluated methods.
Compared with regular fine-tuning, it improves LiveCodeBench
pass@1 by 10.86 percentage points for Qwen and 6.29 points for GLM.
